Virginia Woolf. The British modernist novelist whose works pioneered stream-of-consciousness technique and feminist literary theory.

Born into an intellectual London family in 1882, Woolf belonged to the Bloomsbury circle, an elite intellectual group in early twentieth-century London. She married Leonard Woolf, a writer and political theorist. Throughout her life, she suffered recurring episodes of severe mental illness, likely bipolar disorder, including suicide attempts. Her psychological struggles informed the introspective, fragmented nature of her prose. She was a founding feminist literary theorist. Her essay A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that women need economic and social independence to create art. It remains a foundational text in feminist criticism. In 1941, during a depressive episode, she drowned herself, leaving a suicide note to her husband.

Her major novels include Mrs. Dalloway, published in 1925. This novel inhabits a single day in the consciousness of Clarissa Dalloway, an upper-class London woman. Time is psychological rather than chronological. The narrative parallels her internal world with that of Septimus Warren Smith. To the Lighthouse appeared in 1927. A family's journey to a lighthouse unfolds across decades, structured in three parts—"The Window," "Time Passes," and "The Lighthouse." The novel explores time, motherhood, and mortality with unprecedented subtlety. Orlando, published in 1928, is a fantastical biography spanning three hundred years. The protagonist changes sex midway through the narrative, offering playful gender commentary and parody of biographical convention. The Waves came out in 1931. Six characters' inner monologues appear in a poetic, rhythmic form. There is no external action, only the ebb and flow of thought and emotion.

Woolf is a master of stream-of-consciousness narration—interior monologue capturing the simultaneous flow of perception, memory, and emotion. She dissolves traditional plot entirely. Time becomes subjective and fluid. Five minutes of conversation might span pages; years might become a single paragraph. Her prose is poetic and rhythmic, influenced by modernist poetry and musical form. Repetition and metaphorical coherence matter more than narrative coherence. She valorizes the ordinary and domestic—a woman's morning, a family's weekend, the texture of daily consciousness—elevating it to high art.

Woolf's career marks a decisive moment in modernism: the assertion that women's interiority and ordinary domestic life are worthy of the most demanding literary forms. She insisted, in both her novels and essays, that women's minds and experiences were equal to those of men. Her stream-of-consciousness technique, developed parallel to Joyce's, asks not "what happened?" but "what did it feel like?" Her influence extends through feminist literary criticism, where she remains canonical. She represents both modernism's technical apex and the moment modernism became intertwined with feminist consciousness.
